newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turks celebrate first tanker loading for Iraq oil.
newsitem.headline: Turks celebrate first tanker loading for Iraq oil.

text.p: Iraqi crude oil flowed through this Turkish port on Monday under the U.N. oil-for-food deal after after a six-year break which damaged Ankara's trade with Baghdad.
Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, accompanied by Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, was on hand to give the order: "Begin the petrol operation."
Ceyhan port is terminus of the 986-km (616-mile) twin pipeline from Kirkuk in Northern Iraq that has been shut since 1990 under U.N. sanctions since the invasion of Kuwait.
Erbakan's order enabled the a tanker, loaded with 153,500 tonnes of Iraqi crude bought by Turkey's state refinery Tupras, to leave the port for the Aliaga refinery in western Turkey.
The U.N. deal allows Iraq to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine.

"This is only a beginning, a beginning for the development of southeast Anatolia," Erbakan said of Turkey's southeast, which borders Iraq and has been severely hit by the loss of trade with Iraq in the past six years.
Iraq was Turkey's third biggest trade partner before 1990.
"This is not just the opening of a pipeline. We will be sending goods to Iraq. This means bringing life to the southeast region," he said .

Turkish food and medicine suppliers, benefiting from geographical proximity to Iraq, have been lobbying in Iraq since the summer to have the lion's share from Iraq's purchases of humanitarian goods, which will be worth about $1.32 billion.

Turkey said it had lost about $2.5 billion through the shutdown of the pipeline under the U.N. embargo alone. Officials say Turkey's total trade losses from Iraq, its top oil supplier before the Gulf crisis, amounted to $27 billion.
Tupras, one of the several companies which intended to buy Iraqi crude under the U.N. deal, has agreed to purchase 75,000 barrels per day (bpd) from the terminal.
Fatih Sen, regional director of the state pipeline company Botas, said another tanker of "foreign" origin would arrive at the port to lift Iraqi oil, but he gave no details.
"We hope this will be the beginning of the end for the suffering for Iraq's people," Rafi Dahham Mijwel al-Tiqriti, Iraq's ambassador to Ankara, told Reuters.
Iraq pumped an average 1.5 million bpd of oil, or nearly two-thirds of its total oil exports, through the pipeline before the U.N. embargo. Sanctions on Baghdad remain in place.

Hundreds of supporters of Erbakan's Welfare Party (RP) brought in from Erbakan's hometown of Konya overnight shouted slogans including "Mucahit (Holy Warrior) Erbakan" and slaughtered two sheep at the terminal premises where about 3,000 people gathered to mark the occasion.
Schoolgirls performed folk dances in the muddy fields overlooking the jetty.
